result:
Outside the laundromat, someone has zip-tied a colander to a drainpipe and planted mint in it. The colander is the old enamel kind, white with a blue rim. A few of the leaves have grown through the holes.

I noticed it on a day when I had managed to dye all my white socks a pale, uneven pink. I was standing on the pavement with one of them stretched over my hand, as if better light might exonerate it. A woman coming out of the laundromat stopped beside me.

“Salmon,” she said.

I thought she meant the sock. “You think?”

“No, I mean that’s what I use the mint for.” She pinched off a sprig. “The sock’s pink.”

I liked her for not trying to cheer me up.

The socks have lasted years. Apparently whatever makes a sock indestructible also makes it particularly receptive to a red tea towel. I wore a pair to a wedding last spring, under a charcoal suit. In the photographs you can see a narrow pink stripe between my trousers and my shoes. My sister says it looks deliberate.

The mint is still there, too. This morning I took a few leaves home and chopped them into a bowl of peas. I’ve never tried them with salmon.
